entries.4b3b56a2aabc45f4281ee275944f5e6ca96ed885: <div sID="gen15730" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Isa.11" sID="Isa.11"/> <div eID="gen15730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15731" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15732" type="x-p"/> It is a very good transition in prophecy (whether it be so in rhetoric or no), and a very common one, to pass from the prediction of the temporal deliverances of the church to that of the great salvation, which in the fulness of time should be wrought out by Jesus Christ, of which the other were types and figures, to which all the prophets bore witness; and so the ancient Jews understood them. For what else was it that raised so great an expectation of the Messiah at the time he came. Upon occasion of the prophecy of the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib, here comes in a prophecy concerning Messiah the Prince. I. His rise out of the house of David, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. His qualifications for his great undertaking, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2-Isa.11.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. The justice and equity of his government, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.3-Isa.11.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. IV. The peaceableness of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.6-Isa.11.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. V. The accession of the Gentiles to it (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">ver. 10</reference>), and with them the remnant of the Jews, that should be united with them in the Messiah's kingdom (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.11-Isa.11.16">ver. 11-16</reference>) and of all this God would now shortly give them a type, and some dark representation, in the excellent government of Hezekiah, the great peace which the nation should enjoy under him, after the ruin of Sennacherib's design, and the return of many of the ten tribes out of their dispersion to their brethren of the land of Judah, when they enjoyed that great tranquility.
entries.3bb8a430ecab57a9b9169577ba3e9976929477f5: <div eID="gen15732" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15731" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prophecy of the Messiah; The Government of Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15733" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots: <hi type="super">2</hi> And the spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="super">3</hi> And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears: <hi type="super">4</hi> But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked. <hi type="super">5</hi> And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins. <hi type="super">6</hi> The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den. <hi type="super">9</hi> They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as the waters cover the sea. <div eID="gen15733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15734" type="x-p"/> The prophet had before, in this sermon, spoken of a child that should be born, a son that should be given, on whose shoulders the government should be, intending this for the comfort of the people of God in times of trouble, as dying Jacob, many ages before, had intended the prospect of Shiloh for the comfort of his seed in their affliction in Egypt. He had said (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">ch. x. 27</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the yoke should be destroyed because of the anointing;</hi> now here he tells us on whom that anointing should rest. He foretels, <div eID="gen15734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15735" type="x-p"/> I. That the Messiah should, in due time, arise out of the house of David, as that <hi type="italic">branch</hi> of the Lord which he had said (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">ch. iv. 2</reference>) should be excellent and glorious; the word is <hi type="italic">Netzer,</hi> which some think is referred to in <reference osisRef="Matt.2.23">Matt. ii. 23</reference>, where it is said to be spoken by the prophets of the Messiah that he <hi type="italic">should be called a Nazarene.</hi> Observe here, 1. Whence this branch should arise-from <hi type="italic">Jesse.</hi> He should be the son of David, with whom the covenant of royalty was made, and to whom it was promised with an oath that <hi type="italic">of the fruit of his loins God would raise of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Acts ii. 30</reference>. David is often called <hi type="italic">the son of Jesse,</hi> and Christ is called so, because he was to be not only the Son of David, but David himself, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>. 2. The meanness of his appearance. (1.) He is called a <hi type="italic">rod,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">branch;</hi> both the words here used signify a weak, small, tender product, a <hi type="italic">twig</hi> and a <hi type="italic">sprig</hi> (so some render them), such as is easily broken off. The enemies of God's church were just before compared to strong and stately boughs (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">ch. x. 33</reference>), which will not, without great labour, be hewn down, but Christ to a tender branch (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">ch. liii. 2</reference>); yet he shall be victorious over them. (2.) He is said to come out of Jesse rather than David, because Jesse lived and died in meanness and obscurity; his family was of small account (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.18">1 Sam. xviii. 18</reference>), and it was in a way of contempt and reproach that David was sometimes called the <hi type="italic">son of Jesse,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.7">1 Sam. xxii. 7</reference>. (3.) He comes forth out of the <hi type="italic">stem,</hi> or <hi type="italic">stump,</hi> of Jesse. When the royal family, that had been as a cedar, was cut down, and only the stump of it left, almost levelled with the ground and lost in the grass of the field (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.15">Dan. iv. 15</reference>), yet it shall sprout again (<reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job xiv. 7</reference>); nay, it <hi type="italic">shall grow out of his roots,</hi> which are quite buried in the earth, and, like the roots of flowers in the winter, have no stem appearing above ground. The house of David was reduced and brought very low at the time of Christ's birth, witness the obscurity and poverty of Joseph and Mary. The Messiah was thus to begin his estate of humiliation, for submitting to which he should be highly exalted, and would thus give early notice that his kingdom was not of this world. The Chaldee paraphrase reads this, <hi type="italic">There shall come forth a King from the sons of Jesse, and the Messiah</hi> (or Christ) <hi type="italic">shall be anointed out of his sons' sons.</hi> <div eID="gen15735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15736" type="x-p"/> II. That he should be every way qualified for that great work to which he was designed, that this tender branch should be so watered with the dews of heaven as to become a strong rod for a sceptre to rule, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. In general, <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.</hi> The Holy Spirit, in all his gifts and graces, shall not only come, but rest and abide upon him; he shall have the Spirit not by measure, but without measure, the fulness of the Godhead dwelling in him, <reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col. i. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.9">ii. 9</reference>. He began his preaching with this (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Luke iv. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.</hi> 2. In particular, the spirit of government, by which he should be every way fitted for that judgment which the Father has committed to him and <hi type="italic">given him authority to execute</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">John v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>), and not only so, but should be made the fountain and treasury of all grace to believers, that from his fulness they might all receive the Spirit of grace, as all the members of the body derive animal spirits from the head. (1.) He shall have <hi type="italic">the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and knowledge;</hi> he shall thoroughly understand the business he is to be employed in. <hi type="italic">No man knows the Father but the Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. What he is to make known to the children of men concerning God, and his mind and will, he shall be himself acquainted with and apprised of, <reference osisRef="John.1.18">John i. 18</reference>. He shall know how to administer the affairs of his spiritual kingdom in all the branches of it, so as effectually to answer the two great intentions of it, the glory of God and the welfare of the children of men. The terms of the covenant shall be settled by him, and ordinances instituted, in wisdom: treasures of wisdom shall be hid in him; he shall be our counsellor, and shall be made of God to us wisdom. (2.) <hi type="italic">The spirit of courage,</hi> or <hi type="italic">might,</hi> or fortitude. The undertaking was very great, abundance of difficulty must be broken through, and therefore it was necessary that he should be so endowed that he <hi type="italic">might not fail or be discouraged,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">ch. xlii. 4</reference>. He was famed for courage in his teaching the way of God in truth, and not caring for any man, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.16">Matt. xxii. 16</reference>. (3.) The spirit of religion, or <hi type="italic">the fear of the Lord;</hi> not only he shall himself have a reverent affection for his Father, as his servant (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">ch. xlii. 1</reference>), and he was heard in <hi type="italic">that he feared</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), but he shall have a zeal for religion, and shall design the advancement of it in his whole undertaking. Our faith in Christ was never designed to supersede and jostle out, but to increase and support, our fear of the Lord. <div eID="gen15736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15737" type="x-p"/> III. That he should be accurate, and critical, and very exact in the administration of his government and the exercise of the power committed to him (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">v. 3</reference>): The Spirit wherewith he shall be clothed <hi type="italic">shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the Lord</hi>—of an acute smell or scent (so the word is), for the apprehensions of the mind are often expressed by the sensations of the body. Note, 1. Those are most truly and valuably intelligent that are so in the fear of the Lord, in the business of religion, for that is both the foundation and top-stone of wisdom. 2. By this it will appear that we have the Spirit of God, if we have spiritual senses exercised, and are of <hi type="italic">quick understanding in the fear of the lord.</hi> Those have divine illumination that know their duty and know how to go about it. 3. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> Jesus Christ had the spirit without measure, that he might perfectly understand his undertaking; and he did so, as appears not only in the admirable answers he gave to all that questioned with him, which proved him to be of <hi type="italic">quick understanding in the fear of the Lord,</hi> but in the management of his whole undertaking. He has settled the great affair of religion so unexpectedly well (so as effectually to secure both God's honour and man's happiness) that, it must be owned, he thoroughly understood it. <div eID="gen15737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15738" type="x-p"/> IV. That he should be just and righteous in all the acts of his government, and there should appear in it as much equity as wisdom. He shall judge as he expresses it himself, and as he himself would be judged of, <reference osisRef="John.7.24">John vii. 24</reference>. 1. Not according to outward appearance (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes,</hi> with respect of persons (<reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job xxxiv. 19</reference>) and according to outward shows and appearances, not <hi type="italic">reprove after the hearing of his ears,</hi> by common fame and report, and the representations of others, as men commonly do; nor does he judge of men by the fair words they speak, <hi type="italic">calling him, Lord, Lord,</hi> or their plausible actions before the eye of the world, which they do to be seen of men; but he will judge by the hidden man of the heart, and the inward principles men are governed by, of which he is an infallible witness. Christ will judge the secrets of men (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.16">Rom. ii. 16</reference>), will determine concerning them, not according to their own pretensions and appearances (that were to <hi type="italic">judge after the sight of the eyes</hi>), not according to the opinion others have of them (that were to judge after the hearing of the ears), but we are sure that <hi type="italic">his judgment is according to truth.</hi> 2. He will judge righteous judgment (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins.</hi> He shall be righteous in the administration of his government, and his righteousness shall be his girdle; it shall constantly compass him and cleave to him, shall be his ornament and honour; he shall gird himself for every action, shall gird on his sword for war in righteousness; his righteousness shall be his strength, and shall make him expeditious in his undertakings, as a man with his loins girt. In conformity to Christ, his followers must have the girdle of truth (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.14">Eph. vi. 14</reference>) and it will be the stability of the times. Particularly, (1.) He shall in righteousness plead for the people that are poor and oppressed; he will be their protector (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">With righteousness shall he judge the poor;</hi> he shall judge in favour and defence of those that have right on their side, though they are poor in the world, and because they are poor in spirit. It is the duty of princes to defend and deliver the poor (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.3-Ps.82.4">Ps. lxxxii. 3, 4</reference>), and the honour of Christ that he is the poor man's King, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Ps. lxxii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">4</reference>. He shall <hi type="italic">debate with evenness for the meek of the earth,</hi> or of the land; those that bear the injuries done them with meekness and patience are in a special manner entitled to the divine care and protection. <hi type="italic">I, as a deaf man, heard not, for thou wilt hear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13-Ps.38.14">Ps. xxxviii. 13, 14</reference>. Some read it, <hi type="italic">He shall reprove or correct the meek of the earth with equity.</hi> If his own people, the meek of the land, do amiss, he will <hi type="italic">visit their transgression with the rod.</hi> (2.) He shall in righteousness plead against his enemies that are proud and oppressors (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">But he shall smite the earth,</hi> the man of the earth, that doth oppress (see <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">Ps. x. 18</reference>), the men of the world, that <hi type="italic">mind earthly things</hi> only (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>); these he shall smite <hi type="italic">with the rod of his mouth,</hi> the word of his mouth, speaking terror and ruin to them; his threatenings shall take hold of them, and be executed upon them. <hi type="italic">With the breath of his lips,</hi> by the operation of his Spirit, according to his word, and working with and by it, <hi type="italic">he shall slay the wicked.</hi> He will do it easily, with a word's speaking, as he laid those flat who came to seize him, by saying <hi type="italic">I am he,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.6">John xviii. 6</reference>. Killing terrors shall arrest their consciences, killing judgments shall ruin them, their power, and all their interests; and in the other world everlasting tribulation will be recompensed to those that trouble his poor people. The apostle applies this to the destruction of the man of sin, whom he calls <hi type="italic">that wicked one</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2 Thess. ii. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">whom the Lord will consume with the spirit of his mouth.</hi> And the Chaldee here reads it, <hi type="italic">He shall slay that wicked Romulus,</hi> or Rome, as Mr. Hugh Broughton understands it. <div eID="gen15738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15739" type="x-p"/> V. That there should be great peace and tranquillity under his government; this is an explication of what was said in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">ch. ix. 6</reference>, that he should be the Prince of peace. Peace signifies two things:— <div eID="gen15739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15740" type="x-p"/> 1. Unity or concord, which is intimated in these figurative promises, that even <hi type="italic">the wolf shall dwell</hi> peaceably <hi type="italic">with the lamb;</hi> men of the most fierce and furious dispositions, who used to bite and devour all about them, shall have their temper so strangely altered by the efficacy of the gospel and grace of Christ that they shall live in love even with the weakest and such as formerly they would have made an easy prey of. So far shall the sheep be from hurting one another, as sometimes they have done (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.20-Ezek.34.21">Ezek. xxxiv. 20, 21</reference>), that even the wolves shall agree with them. Christ, who is our peace, came to slay all enmities and to settle lasting friendships among his followers, particularly between Jews and Gentiles: when multitudes of both, being converted to the faith of Christ, united in one sheep-fold, then the wolf and the lamb dwelt together; the wolf did not so much as threaten the lamb, nor was the lamb afraid of the wolf. <hi type="italic">The leopard shall</hi> not only not tear the kid, but shall <hi type="italic">lie down with her:</hi> even <hi type="italic">their young ones shall lie down together,</hi> and shall be trained up in a blessed amity, in order to the perpetuating of it. <hi type="italic">The lion</hi> shall cease to be ravenous and <hi type="italic">shall eat straw like the ox,</hi> as some think all the beasts of prey did before the fall. <hi type="italic">The asp</hi> and <hi type="italic">the cockatrice</hi> shall cease to be venomous, so that parents shall let their children <hi type="italic">play</hi> with them and <hi type="italic">put their hands</hi> among them. A generation of vipers shall become a seed of saints, and the old complaint of <hi type="italic">homo homini lupus—man is a wolf to man,</hi> shall be at an end. Those that inhabit the holy mountain shall live as amicably as the creatures did that were with Noah in the ark, and it shall be a means of their preservation, for <hi type="italic">they shall not hurt nor destroy</hi> one another as they have done. Now, (1.) This is fulfilled in the wonderful effect of the gospel upon the minds of those that sincerely embrace it; it changes the nature, and makes those that trampled on the meek of the earth, not only meek like them, but affectionate towards them. When Paul, who had persecuted the saints, joined himself to them, then the <hi type="italic">wolf dwelt with the lamb.</hi> (2.) Some are willing to hope it shall yet have a further accomplishment in the latter days, when <hi type="italic">swords shall be beaten into ploughshares.</hi> <div eID="gen15740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15741" type="x-p"/> 2. Safety or security. Christ, the great Shepherd, shall take such care of the flock that those who would hurt them shall not; they shall not only not destroy one another, but no enemy from without shall be permitted to give them any molestation. The property of troubles, and of death itself, shall be so altered that they shall not do any real hurt to, much less shall they be the destruction of, any that <hi type="italic">have their conversation in the holy mountain,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.13">1 Pet. iii. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who,</hi> or what, <hi type="italic">can harm us, if we be followers of him that is good?</hi> God's people shall be delivered, not only from evil, but from the fear of it. Even <hi type="italic">the sucking child</hi> shall without any terror <hi type="italic">play upon the hole of the asp;</hi> blessed Paul does so when he says, <hi type="italic">Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?</hi> and, <hi type="italic">O death! where is thy sting?</hi> <div eID="gen15741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15742" type="x-p"/> Lastly, Observe what shall be the effect, and what the cause, of this wonderful softening and sweetening of men's tempers by the grace of God. 1. The effect of it shall be tractableness, and a willingness to receive instruction: <hi type="italic">A little child shall lead those</hi> who formerly scorned to be controlled by the strongest man. Calvin understands it of their willing submission to the ministers of Christ, who are to instruct with meekness and not to use any coercive power, but to be as <hi type="italic">little children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.18.3">Matt. xviii. 3</reference>. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.5">2 Cor. viii. 5</reference>. 2. The cause of it shall be the knowledge of God. The more there is of that the more there is of a disposition to peace. They shall thus live in love, <hi type="italic">for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord,</hi> which shall extinguish men's heats and animosities. The better acquainted we are with the God of love the more shall we be changed into the same image and the better affected shall we be to all those that bear his image. The earth shall be as full of this knowledge as the channels of the sea are of water—so broad and extensive shall this knowledge be and so far shall it spread—so deep and substantial shall this knowledge be, and so long shall it last. There is much more of the knowledge of God to be got by the gospel of Christ than could be got by the law of Moses; and, whereas <hi type="italic">then</hi> in <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> only was God known, now <hi type="italic">all shall know him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.11">Heb. viii. 11</reference>. But that is knowledge falsely so called which sows discord among men; the right knowledge of God settles peace.
entries.2315217e558d694e68e8ccd6c87fcbd52d5034f4: <div eID="gen15742" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Advancement of Messiah's Kingdom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15743" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. <hi type="super">13</hi> The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim. <hi type="super">14</hi> But they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines toward the west; they shall spoil them of the east together: they shall lay their hand upon Edom and Moab; and the children of Ammon shall obey them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make <hi type="italic">men</hi> go over dry-shod. <hi type="super">16</hi> And there shall be a highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria; like as it was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt. <div eID="gen15743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15744" type="x-p"/> We have here a further prophecy of the enlargement and advancement of the kingdom of the Messiah, under the type and figure of the flourishing condition of the kingdom of Judah in the latter end of Hezekiah's reign, after the defeat of Sennacherib. <div eID="gen15744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15745" type="x-p"/> I. This prediction was in part accomplished when the great things God did for Hezekiah and his people proved as an ensign, inviting the neighbouring nations to them <hi type="italic">to enquire of the wonders done in the land,</hi> on which errand the king of Babylon's ambassadors came. To them the Gentiles sought; and Jerusalem, the rest or habitation of the Jews, was then glorious, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">v. 10</reference>. Then many of the Israelites who belonged to the kingdom of the ten tribes, who upon the destruction of that kingdom by the king of Assyria were forced to flee for shelter into all the countries about and to some that lay very remote, even to the islands of the sea, were encouraged to return to their own country and put themselves under the protection and government of the king of Judah, the rather because it was an Assyrian army by which their country had been ruined and that was not routed. This is said to be a recovery of them <hi type="italic">the second time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">v. 11</reference>), such an instance of the power and goodness of God, and such a reviving to them, as their first deliverance out of Egypt was. Then the <hi type="italic">outcasts of Israel</hi> should be gathered in, and brought home, and those of Judah too, who, upon the approach of the Assyrian army, shifted for their own safety. Then the old feud between Ephraim and Judah shall be forgotten, and they shall join against the Philistines and their other common enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.13-Isa.11.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Note, Those who have been sharers with each other in afflictions and mercies, dangers and deliverances, ought in consideration thereof to unite for their joint and mutual safety and protection; and it is likely to be well with the church when Ephraim and Judah are one against the Philistines. Then, whatever difficulties there may be in the way of the return of the dispersed, the Lord shall find out some way or other to remove them, as when he brought Israel out of Egypt he dried up the Red Sea and Jordan (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">v. 15</reference>) and led them to Canaan through the invincible embarrassments of a vast howling wilderness, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.16">v. 16</reference>. The like will he do this second time, or that which shall be equivalent. When God's time has come for the deliverance of his people mountains of opposition shall become plain before him. Let us not despair therefore when the interests of the church seem to be brought very low; God can soon turn gloomy days into glorious ones. <div eID="gen15745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15746" type="x-p"/> II. It had a further reference to the days of the Messiah and the accession of the Gentiles to his kingdom; for to these the apostle applies <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">v. 10</reference>, of which the following verses are a continuation. <reference osisRef="Rom.15.12">Rom. xv. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">There shall be a root of Jesse; and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles, in him shall the Gentiles trust.</hi> That is a key to this prophecy, which speaks of Christ as the root of Jesse, or <hi type="italic">a branch out of his roots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">a root out of a dry ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">ch. liii. 2</reference>. He is the <hi type="italic">root of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.5">Rev. v. 5</reference>), the <hi type="italic">root and offspring of David</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Rev. xxii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen15746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15747" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">He shall stand,</hi> or be set up, <hi type="italic">for an ensign of the people.</hi> When he was crucified he was <hi type="italic">lifted up from the earth,</hi> that, as an ensign of beacon, he might <hi type="italic">draw</hi> the eyes and the hearts of <hi type="italic">all men unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.32">John xii. 32</reference>. He is set up as an ensign in the preaching of the everlasting gospel, in which the ministers, as standard-bearers, display the banner of his love, to allure us to him (<reference osisRef="Song.1.4">Cant. i. 4</reference>), the banner of his truth, under which we may enlist ourselves, to engage in a holy war against sin and Satan. Christ is the ensign to which <hi type="italic">the children of God that were scattered abroad are gathered together</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.51">John xi. 51</reference>), and in him they meet as the centre of their unity. <div eID="gen15747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15748" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">To him shall the Gentiles seek.</hi> We read of Greeks that did so (<reference osisRef="John.12.21">John xii. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">We would see Jesus</hi>), and upon that occasion Christ spoke of his being lifted up, to draw all men to him. The apostle, from the LXX. (or perhaps the LXX. from the apostle, in the editions after Christ) reads it (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.12">Rom. xv. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">In him shall the Gentiles trust;</hi> they shall seek to him with a dependence on him. <div eID="gen15748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15749" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">His rest shall be glorious.</hi> Some understand this of the death of Christ (the triumphs of the cross made even that glorious), others of his ascension, when he sat down to rest at the right hand of God. Or rather it is meant of the gospel church, that Mount Zion of which Christ has said, <hi type="italic">This is my rest,</hi> and in which he resides. This, though despised by the world, having upon it the beauty of holiness, is truly glorious, a <hi type="italic">glorious high throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">Jer. xvii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen15749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15750" type="x-p"/> 4. Both Jews and Gentiles shall be gathered to him, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">v. 11</reference>. A remnant of both, a little remnant in comparison, which shall be recovered, as it were, with great difficulty and hazard. As formerly God delivered his people, and gathered them out of all the countries whither they were scattered (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Ps. cvi. 47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15-Jer.16.16">Jer. xvi. 15, 16</reference>), so he will a second time, in another way, by the powerful working of the Spirit of grace with the word. He <hi type="italic">shall set his hand</hi> to do it; he shall exert his power, the <hi type="italic">arm of the Lord shall be revealed</hi> to do it. (1.) There shall be a remnant of the Jews gathered in: <hi type="italic">The outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">v. 12</reference>), many of whom, at the time of the bringing of them in to Christ, were <hi type="italic">Jews of the dispersion, the twelve tribes that were scattered abroad</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.1">James i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.1">1 Pet. i. 1</reference>), shall flock to Christ; and probably more of those scattered Jews were brought into the church, in proportion, than of those which remained in their own land. (2.) Many of <hi type="italic">the nations,</hi> the Gentiles, shall be brought in by the lifting up of the ensign. Jacob foretold concerning Shiloh that <hi type="italic">to him should the gathering of the people be.</hi> Those that were strangers and foreigners shall be made nigh. The Jews were jealous of Christ's going to the dispersed among the Gentiles and of his <hi type="italic">teaching the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.35">John vii. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen15750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15751" type="x-p"/> 5. There shall be a happy accommodation between Judah and Ephraim, and both shall be safe from their adversaries and have dominion over them, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.13-Isa.11.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. The coalescence between Judah and Israel at that time was a type and figure of the uniting of Jews and Gentiles, who had been so long at variance in the gospel church. <hi type="italic">The house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jer. iii. 18</reference>) and become <hi type="italic">one nation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.22">Ezek. xxxvii. 22</reference>); so the Jews and Gentiles are made of <hi type="italic">twain one new man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Eph. ii. 15</reference>), and, being at peace one with another, those that are adversaries to them both shall be cut off; for <hi type="italic">they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines,</hi> as an eagle strikes at her prey, shall spoil those on the west side of them, and then they shall extend their conquests eastward over the Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites. The gospel of Christ shall be successful in all parts, and some of all nations shall become obedient to the faith. <div eID="gen15751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15752" type="x-p"/> 6. Every thing that might hinder the progress and success of the gospel shall be taken out of the way. As when God brought Israel out of Egypt he dried up the Red Sea and Jordan before them (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.11-Isa.63.12">ch. lxiii. 11, 12</reference>), and as afterwards when he brought up the Jews out of Babylon he <hi type="italic">prepared them their way</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.10">ch. lxii. 10</reference>), so when Jews and Gentiles are to be brought together into the gospel church all obstructions shall be removed (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.15-Isa.11.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), difficulties that seemed insuperable shall be strangely got over, <hi type="italic">the blind shall be led by a way that they knew not.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.42.15-Isa.42.16">ch. xlii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.19-Isa.43.20">xliii. 19, 20</reference>. Converts shall be brought in chariots and in litters, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.20">ch. lxvi. 20</reference>. Some think it is the further accession of multitudes to the church that is pointed at in that obscure prophecy of the drying up of the river Euphrates, that the way of the kings of the east may be prepared (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.12">Rev. xvi. 12</reference>), which seems to refer to this prophecy. Note, When God's time has come for the bringing of nations, or particular persons, home to himself, divine grace will be victorious over all opposition. At the presence of the Lord the sea shall flee and Jordan be driven back; and those who set their faces heavenward will find there are not such difficulties in the way as they thought there were, for there is a highway thither, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">ch. xxxv. 8</reference>.  <chapter eID="Isa.11"/> <div eID="gen15752" type="x-p"/>

entries.1167c236ee4afbf0672125474b47ada9610e8f67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8527"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen13882" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.16">Is 11:1-16</reference>.<div eID="gen13882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">From the local and temporary national deliverance the prophet passes by the law of suggestion in an easy transition to the end of all prophecy--</hi>the everlasting deliverance under Messiah's reign, not merely His first coming, but chiefly His second coming. The language and illustrations are still drawn from the temporary national subject, with which he began, but the glories described pertain to Messiah's reign. Hezekiah cannot, as some think, be the subject; for he was already come, whereas the "stem of Jesse" was yet future ("shall come") (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11">Mi 4:11</reference>, &c.; 5:1, 2; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">33:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.12">Ro 15:12</reference>).<div eID="gen13883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8527"/><hi type="bold">1. rod--</hi>When the proud "boughs" of "Lebanon" (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">Is 10:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">34</reference>, the Assyrians) are lopped, and the vast "forests cut down" amidst all this rage, a seemingly humble rod shall come out of Jesse (Messiah), who shall retrieve the injuries done by the Assyrian "rod" to Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>, 6, 18, 19).<div eID="gen13884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stem--</hi>literally, "the stump" of a tree cut close by the roots: happily expressing the depressed state of the royal house of David, owing to the hostile storm (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">Is 10:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.19">19</reference>), when Messiah should arise from it, to raise it to more than its pristine glory. <reference osisRef="Luke.2.7">Lu 2:7</reference> proves this (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.14.8">8</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Is 8:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Branch--</hi>Scion. He is nevertheless also the "root" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Is 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.5">Re 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">22:16</reference>. "Root and offspring" combines both, <reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">6:12</reference>). <div eID="gen13886" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e5b803197a259d6dd3e2121c410ae63d2682756: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8528"/><div sID="gen13887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8528"/><hi type="bold">2. Spirit of the Lord--</hi>Jehovah. The Spirit by which the prophets spake: for Messiah was to be a Prophet (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">De 18:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.18">18</reference>). Seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are specified, to imply that the perfection of them was to be in Him. Compare "the seven Spirits" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>), that is, the Holy Ghost in His perfect fulness: seven being the sacred number. The prophets had only a portion out of the "fulness" in the Son of God (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>; 3:34; <reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen13887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rest--</hi>permanently; not merely come upon Him (<reference osisRef="Num.11.25">Nu 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen13888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">Ep 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding--</hi>coupled with "wisdom," being its fruit. Discernment and discrimination (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.18">Mt 22:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.2.25">Joh 2:25</reference>).<div eID="gen13890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">counsel ... might--</hi>the faculty of forming counsels, and that of executing them (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Is 28:29</reference>). Counsellor (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>of the deep things of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Mt 11:27</reference>). The knowledge of Him gives us true knowledge (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">Ep 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen13892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear of the Lord--</hi>reverential, obedient fear. The first step towards true "knowledge" (<reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference>). <div eID="gen13893" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d96726db5f1fd1c138282d8fc3f67be9e503690: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8529"/><div sID="gen13894" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8529"/><hi type="bold">3. make him of quick understanding--</hi>literally, "quick-scented in the fear of Jehovah"; endowed with a singular sagacity in discerning the genuine principle of religious fear of God, when it lies dormant in the yet unawakened sinner (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.20">Mt 12:20</reference>; Ac 10:1-48; 16:14) [Horsley]. But Maurer, "He shall delight in the fear of God." The Hebrew means "to delight in the odors" of anything (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.38">Ex 30:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">Am 5:21</reference>); "smell," that is, "delight in."<div eID="gen13894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after ... sight--</hi>according to mere external appearances (<reference osisRef="John.7.24">Joh 7:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.15">8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">Jas 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>). Herein Messiah is represented a just Judge and Ruler (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.16">De 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen13895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reprove--</hi>"decide," as the parallelism shows.<div eID="gen13896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after ... ears--</hi>by mere plausible hearsays, but by the true merits of each case (<reference osisRef="John.6.64">Joh 6:64</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Re 2:23</reference>). <div eID="gen13897" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ed18a3e611e97aefbcb6bd29e4b712c1a1ad74b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8530"/><div sID="gen13898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8530"/><hi type="bold">4. judge--</hi>see that impartial justice is done them. "Judge" may mean here "rule," as in <reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">Psa 67:4</reference>.<div eID="gen13898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reprove--</hi>or, "argue"; "decide." But Lowth, "work conviction in."<div eID="gen13899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth--</hi>Compare with <reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mt 5:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>.<div eID="gen13900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth--</hi>its ungodly inhabitants, answering to "the wicked" in the parallel, and in antithesis to the "poor" and "meek," namely, in spirit, the humble pious (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.3">Mt 5:3</reference>). It is at the same time implied that "the earth" will be extraordinarily wicked when He shall come to judge and reign. His reign shall therefore be ushered in with judgments on the apostates (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.9-Ps.2.12">Psa 2:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Lu 18:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Re 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen13901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rod of ... mouth--</hi>condemning sentences which proceed from His mouth against the wicked (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.16">Re 1:16</reference>; 2:16; 19:15, 21).<div eID="gen13902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breath of ... lips--</hi>his judicial decisions (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.28">Is 30:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">Re 19:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.9-Rev.20.12">20:9-12</reference>). He as the Word of God (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.13-Rev.19.15">Re 19:13-15</reference>) comes to strike that blow which shall decide His claim to the kingdom, previously usurped by Satan, and "the beast" to whom Satan delegates his power. It will be a day of judgment to the Gentile dispensation, as the first coming was to the Jews. Compare a type of the "rod" (<reference osisRef="Num.17.2-Num.17.10">Nu 17:2-10</reference>). <div eID="gen13903" type="x-p"/>
entries.a23e70980b77883b2cc41ec5f9e10679555c2c3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8531"/><div sID="gen13904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8531"/><hi type="bold">5. righteousness ... girdle--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.1.13">Re 1:13</reference>; 19:11). The antitypical High Priest (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.4">Ex 28:4</reference>). The girdle secures firmly the rest of the garments (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.13">1Pe 1:13</reference>). So "truth" gives firm consistency to the whole character (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Is 59:17</reference>, "righteousness" is His breastplate. <div eID="gen13904" type="x-p"/>
entries.d97844411a01387c20365f36e22842f8ca06ba83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8532"/><div sID="gen13905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8532"/><hi type="bold">6. wolf ... lamb--</hi>Each animal is coupled with that one which is its natural prey. A fit state of things under the "Prince of Peace" (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.25">Is 65:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25">Eze 34:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>). These may be figures for men of corresponding animal-like characters (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.27">Eze 22:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.13">38:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jr 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">13:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.15">Mt 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.3">Lu 10:3</reference>). Still a literal change in the relations of animals to man and each other, restoring the state in Eden, is a more likely interpretation. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.2.19">Ge 2:19</reference>, 20, with <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6-Ps.8.8">Psa 8:6-8</reference>, which describes the restoration to man, in the person of "the Son of man," of the lost dominion over the animal kingdom of which he had been designed to be the merciful vicegerent under God, for the good of his animal subjects (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.19-Rom.8.22">Ro 8:19-22</reference>). <div eID="gen13905" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5daa2bd55c79d63629381c3ad21fc99fa55ab3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8533"/><div sID="gen13906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8533"/><hi type="bold">7. feed--</hi>namely, "together"; taken from the second clause.<div eID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">straw--</hi>no longer flesh and blood. <div eID="gen13907" type="x-p"/>
entries.e752d5ccbe5da79d29e8f592b07d9d0d23a57250: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8534"/><div sID="gen13908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8534"/><hi type="bold">8. play--</hi>literally, "delight" himself in sport.<div eID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cockatrice--</hi>a fabulous serpent supposed to be hatched from the egg of a cock. The Hebrew means a kind of adder, more venomous than the asp; Bochart supposes the basilisk to be meant, which was thought to poison even with its breath. <div eID="gen13909" type="x-p"/>
entries.98aadd849512c54f74e1f59c7f3fd50b9b90f590: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8535"/><div sID="gen13910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8535"/><hi type="bold">9. my holy mountain--</hi>Zion, that is, Jerusalem. The seat of government and of Messiah's throne is put for the whole earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen13910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sea--</hi>As the waters find their way into every cavern of its depths, so Christianity shall pervade every recess of the earth (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">Ha 2:14</reference>). As <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.5">Is 11:1-5</reference> describe the personal qualities of Messiah, and <reference osisRef="Isa.11.6-Isa.11.9">Is 11:6-9</reference> the regenerating effects of His coming on creation, so <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10-Isa.11.16">Is 11:10-16</reference> the results of it in the restoration of His people, the Jews, and the conversion through them of the Gentiles. <div eID="gen13911" type="x-p"/>
entries.d305528b96eabf8bc4d3c3d7d10f6ab9ec0f0a63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8536"/><div sID="gen13912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8536"/><hi type="bold">10. root--</hi>rather, "shoot from the root" (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.5">Re 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">22:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand--</hi>permanently and prominently, as a banner lifted up to be the rallying point of an army or people (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">Joh 12:32</reference>).<div eID="gen13913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the people--</hi>peoples, answering to "the Gentiles" in the parallel member.<div eID="gen13914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to it ... seek--</hi>diligently (<reference osisRef="Job.8.5">Job 8:5</reference>). They shall give in their allegiance to the Divine King (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>; 60:5; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.11">Zec 2:11</reference>). Horsley translates, "Of Him shall the Gentiles inquire"; namely, in a religious sense, resort as to an oracle for consultation in difficulties" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.15.12">Ro 15:12</reference>, which quotes this passage, "In Him shall the Gentiles trust."<div eID="gen13915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13916" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rest--</hi>resting-place (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.13">Is 60:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.8">Psa 132:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>). The sanctuary in the temple of Jerusalem was "the resting-place of the ark and of Jehovah." So the glorious Church which is to be is described under the image of an oracle to which all nations shall resort, and which shall be filled with the visible glory of God. <div eID="gen13916" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9bdc3de4611b13bc5293c758b9c1675a6676951: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8537"/><div sID="gen13917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8537"/><hi type="bold">11. set ... hand--</hi>take in hand the work. Therefore the coming restoration of the Jews is to be distinct from that after the Babylonish captivity, and yet to resemble it. The first restoration was literal, therefore so shall the second be; the latter, however, it is implied here, shall be much more universal than the former (Is 43:5-7; 49:12, 17, 18; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.21">Eze 37:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Am 9:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6">Mi 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.19">Zep 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.10">Zec 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">Jr 23:8</reference>). As to the "remnant" destined by God to survive the judgments on the nation, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.46.28">Jr 46:28</reference>.<div eID="gen13917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pathros--</hi>one of the three divisions of Egypt, Upper Egypt.<div eID="gen13918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cush--</hi>either Ethiopia, south of Egypt, now Abyssinia, or the southern parts of Arabia, along the Red Sea.<div eID="gen13919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Elam--</hi>Persia, especially the southern part of it now called Susiana.<div eID="gen13920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shinar--</hi>Babylonian Mesopotamia, the plain between the Euphrates and the Tigris: in it Babel was begun (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Ge 10:10</reference>). In the Assyrian inscriptions Rawlinson distinguishes three periods: (1) The Chaldean; from 2300 B.C. to 1500, in which falls Chedorlaomer (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.1-Gen.14.17">Ge 14:1-17</reference>), called in the cuneiform characters Kudur of Hur, or Ur of the Chaldees, and described as the conqueror of Syria. The seat of the first Chaldean empire was in the south, towards the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates. (2) The Assyrian, down to 625 B.C. (3) The Babylonian, from 625 to 538 B.C., when Babylon was taken by the Persian Cyrus.<div eID="gen13921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">islands of ... sea--</hi>the far western regions beyond the sea [Jerome]. <div eID="gen13922" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2954884854716c1e3a558fb79e494cda62d0601: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8538"/><div sID="gen13923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8538"/>12. In the first restoration Judah alone was restored, with perhaps some few of Israel (the ten tribes): in the future restoration both are expressly specified (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.16-Ezek.37.19">Eze 37:16-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jr 3:18</reference>). To Israel are ascribed the "outcasts" (masculine); to Judah the "dispersed" (feminine), as the former have been longer and more utterly castaways (though not finally) than the latter (<reference osisRef="John.7.52">Joh 7:52</reference>). The masculine and feminine conjoined express the universality of the restoration.<div eID="gen13923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the four corners of the earth--</hi>Hebrew, "wings of the earth." <div eID="gen13924" type="x-p"/>
entries.28c8a63d152e1d971b7969dfdbb9f781bf2ec9c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8539"/><div sID="gen13925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8539"/><hi type="bold">13. envy ... of Ephraim ... Judah--</hi>which began as early as the time (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.1">Jud 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.12.1">12:1</reference>, &c.). Joshua had sprung from, and resided among the Ephraimites (<reference osisRef="Num.13.9">Nu 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.19.50">Jos 19:50</reference>); the sanctuary was with them for a time (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>). The jealousy increased subsequently (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.8">2Sa 2:8</reference>, &c.; 19:41; 20:<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">2; 3:10</reference>); and even before David's time (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.8">1Sa 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.4">15:4</reference>), they had appropriated to themselves the national name Israel. It ended in disruption (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.26">1Ki 11:26</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.33">1Ki 12:1-33</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.9">2Ki 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56-Ps.78.71">Psa 78:56-71</reference>).<div eID="gen13925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adversaries of Judah--</hi>rather, "the adversaries from Judah"; those of Judah hostile to the Ephraimites [Maurer]. The parallelism "the envy of Ephraim," namely, against Judah, requires this, as also what follows; namely, "Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.15">Eze 37:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.19">17, 19</reference>). <div eID="gen13926" type="x-p"/>
entries.75e61e217250664b46289bcc8a85d0cef4ac964f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8540"/><div sID="gen13927" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8540"/>14. With united forces they shall subdue their foes (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.12">Am 9:12</reference>).<div eID="gen13927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fly--</hi>as a bird of prey (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Ha 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen13928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the shoulders--</hi>This expresses an attack made unexpectedly on one from behind. The image is the more apt, as the Hebrew for "shoulders" in <reference osisRef="Num.34.11">Nu 34:11</reference> is used also of a maritime coast ("side of the sea": Hebrew, "shoulder of the sea," Margin). They shall make a sudden victorious descent upon their borders southwest of Judea.<div eID="gen13929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them of the east--</hi>Hebrew, "children of the East," the Arabs, who, always hostile, are not to be reduced under regular government, but are only to be despoiled (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.28">Jr 49:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen13930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lay ... hand upon--</hi>take possession of (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.42">Da 11:42</reference>).<div eID="gen13931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Edom--</hi>south of Judah, from the Dead Sea to the Red Sea; "Moab"--east of Jordan and the Dead Sea.<div eID="gen13932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ammon--</hi>east of Judea, north of Moab, between the Arnon and Jabbok. <div eID="gen13933" type="x-p"/>
entries.60ea4667ef0e2d65da0cff94b1683799bb06b2d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8541"/><div sID="gen13934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8541"/>15. There shall be a second exodus, destined to eclipse even the former one from Egypt in its wonders. So the prophecies elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.22">Psa 68:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.14.22">Ex 14:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.11">Zec 10:11</reference>). The same deliverance furnishes the imagery by which the return from Babylon is described (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">Is 48:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen13934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroy--</hi>literally, "devote," or "doom," that is, dry up; for what God dooms, perishes (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.9">Psa 106:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Nah.1.4">Na 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen13935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tongue--</hi>the Bubastic branch of the Nile [Vitringa]; but as the Nile was not the obstruction to the exodus, it is rather the west tongue or Heroöpolite fork of the Red Sea.<div eID="gen13936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... mighty wind--</hi>such as the "strong east wind" (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.21">Ex 14:21</reference>), by which God made a way for Israel through the Red Sea. The Hebrew for "mighty" means terrible. Maurer translates, "With the terror of His anger"; that is, His terrible anger.<div eID="gen13937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the seven streams--</hi>rather, "shall smite it (divide it by smiting) into seven (many) streams, so as to be easily crossed" [Lowth]. So Cyrus divided the river Gyndes, which retarded his march against Babylon, into three hundred sixty streams, so that even a woman could cross it [Herodotus, 1.189]. "The river" is the Euphrates, the obstruction to Israel's return "from Assyria" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.16">Is 11:16</reference>), a type of all future impediments to the restoration of the Jews.<div eID="gen13938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dry shod--</hi>Hebrew, "in shoes." Even in sandals they should be able to pass over the once mighty river without being wet (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.12">Re 16:12</reference>). <div eID="gen13939" type="x-p"/>

Israel ... Egypt--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">Is 51:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.12">63:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.13">13</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.11"/>

entries.029ed6116cbd1606a69ce08efcb781c69d1531d9: <div eID="gen26997" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26998" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26999" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26999" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26998" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> The Messiah represented as a slender twig shooting up from the root of an old withered stem, which tender plant, so extremely weak in its first appearance, should nevertheless become fruitful and mighty, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.4">Isa 11:1-4</reference>. Great equity of the Messiah's government, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.5">Isa 11:5</reference>. Beautiful assemblages of images by which the great peace and happiness of his kingdom are set forth, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.6-Isa.11.8">Isa 11:6-8</reference>. The extent of his dominion shall be ultimately that of the whole habitable globe, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Isa 11:9</reference>. The prophet, borrowing his imagery from the exodus from Egypt, predicts, with great majesty of language, the future restoration of the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah, (viz., the whole of the twelve tribes of Israel), from their several dispersions, and also that blessed period when both Jews and Gentiles shall assemble under the banner of Jesus, and zealously unite in extending the limits of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10-Isa.11.16">Isa 11:10-16</reference>. <div eID="gen27000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> The prophet had described the destruction of the Assyrian army under the image of a mighty forest, consisting of flourishing trees growing thick together, and of a great height; of Lebanon itself crowned with lofty cedars, but cut down and laid level with the ground by the axe wielded by the hand of some powerful and illustrious agent. In opposition to this image he represents the great Person who makes the subject of this chapter as a slender twig shooting out from the trunk of an old tree, cut down, lopped to the very root, and decayed; which tender plant, so weak in appearance, should nevertheless become fruitful and prosper. This contrast shows plainly the connection between this and the preceding chapter, which is moreover expressed by the connecting particle; and we have here a remarkable instance of that method so common with the prophets, and particularly with Isaiah, of taking occasion, from the mention of some great temporal deliverance, to launch out into the display of the spiritual deliverance of God's people by the Messiah; for that this prophecy relates to the Messiah we have the express authority of St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.12">Rom 15:12</reference>. 'He joins this paragraph, with respect to the days of the Messiah, with the fidelity that was in the days of Hezekiah." - Kimchi, in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference>. Thus in the latter part of Isaiah's prophecies the subject of the great redemption, and of the glories of the Messiah's kingdom, arises out of the restoration of Judah by the deliverance from the captivity of Babylon, and is all along connected and intermixed with it.
entries.daa09e5e87beef89f278098e0023ebe457e76c67: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27002" type="x-p"/> With the rod of his mouth "By the blast of his mouth" - For בשבט beshebet, by the rod, Houbigant reads בשבת beshebeth, by the blast of his mouth, from נשב nashab, to blow. The conjecture is ingenious and probable; and seems to be confirmed by the Septuagint and Chaldee, who render it by the word of his mouth, which answers much better to the correction than to the present reading. Add to this, that the blast of his mouth is perfectly parallel to the breath of his lips in the next line.
entries.68762f639ac280e08bfae5cf949cb400cd629cbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> The girdle "The cincture" - All the ancient Versions, except that of Symmachus, have two different words for girdle in the two hemistichs. It is not probable that Isaiah would have repeated אזור azer, when a synonymous word so obvious as חגור chagor occurred. The tautology seems to have arisen from the mistake of some transcriber. The meaning of this verse is, that a zeal for justice and truth shall make him active and strong in executing the great work which he shall undertake. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.27">Isa 5:27</reference>.
entries.92982ca5712198c10528e31292fa22a73d512371: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> The wolf also shall, etc. "Then shall the wolf," etc. - The idea of the renewal of the golden age, as it is called, is much the same in the Oriental writers with that of the Greeks and Romans: - the wild beasts grow tame; serpents and poisonous herbs become harmless; all is peace and harmony, plenty and happiness: - <div eID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> Occidet et serpens, et fallax herba veneni Occidet. <div eID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> Vega. Eclog. 4:24. "The serpent's brood shall die. The sacred ground <div eID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> Shall weeds and noxious plants refuse to bear." - Nec magnos metuent armenta leones. <div eID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> Virg. Eclog. 4:22. "Nor shall the flocks fear the great lions." <div eID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27009" type="x-p"/> Non lupus insidias explorat ovilia circum, <div eID="gen27009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> Nec gregibus nocturnus obambulat: acrior illum <div eID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> Cura domat: timidae damae cervique fugaces <div eID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> Nunc interque canes, et circum tecta vagantur. <div eID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> Virg. Georg. 3:537. "The nightly wolf that round the enclosure prowled, <div eID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> To leap the fence, now plots not on the fold: <div eID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> Tamed with a sharper pain, the fearful doe <div eID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> And flying stag amidst the greyhounds go; <div eID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> And round the dwellings roam, of man, their former foe." <div eID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> Nec vespertinus circumgemit ursus ovile, <div eID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> Nec intumescit alta viperis humus. <div eID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> Hor. Epod. 16:51. "Nor evening bears the sheepfold growl around, <div eID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27022" type="x-p"/> Nor mining vipers heave the tainted ground." <div eID="gen27022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> Dryden. Εσται δη τουτ' αμαρ, ὁπηνικα νεβρον εν ευνᾳ Καρχαροδων δινεσθαι ιδων λυκος ουκ εθελησει. <div eID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27024" type="x-p"/> Theoc. Idyl. 24:84. <div eID="gen27024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> There shall be a time when the ravenous wolf shall see the kid lying at ease, and shall feel no desire to do it an injury. <div eID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27026" type="x-p"/> I have laid before the reader these common passages from the most elegant of the ancient poets, that he may see how greatly the prophet on the same subject has the advantage upon the comparison; how much the former fall short of that beauty and elegance, and variety of imagery, with which Isaiah has set forth the very same ideas. The wolf and the leopard not only forbear to destroy the lamb and the kid, but even take their abode and lie down together with them. The calf, and the young lion, and the fatling, not only come together, but are led quietly in the same band, and that by a little child. The heifer and the she-bear not only feed together, but even lodge their young ones, for whom they used to be most jealously fearful, in the same place. All the serpent kind is so perfectly harmless, that the sucking infant and the newly weaned child puts his hand on the basilisk's den, and plays upon the hole of the aspic. The lion not only abstains from preying on the weaker animals, but becomes tame and domestic, and feeds on straw like the ox. These are all beautiful circumstances, not one of which has been touched upon by the ancient poets. The Arabian and Persian poets elegantly apply the same ideas to show the effects of justice impartially administered, and firmly supported, by a great and good king: - "Mahmoud the powerful king, the ruler of the world, <div eID="gen27026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> To whose tank the wolf and the lamb come, together to drink." <div eID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27028" type="x-p"/> Ferdusi. "Through the influence of righteousness, the hungry wolf <div eID="gen27028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> Becomes mild, though in the presence of the white kid." <div eID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> Ibn Onein. Jones, Poes. Asiat. Comment., p. 380. <div eID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> The application is extremely ingenious and beautiful: but the exquisite imagery of Isaiah is not equalled.
entries.04d6d1e5761034e4bdb797bfdffba27cd625a45f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> In this verse a word is omitted in the text, יחדו yachdav, together; which ought to be repeated in the second hemistich, being quite necessary to the sense. It is accordingly twice expressed by the Septuagint and Syriac.
entries.bcad97a671dc7f2a2c5b8aaded49abb1a29afdde: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27033" type="x-p"/> The cockatrice' den - This is supposed, both by the Targum and by Kimchi, to mean the pupil of this serpent's eye. "When," says Kimchi, "he is in the mouth of his den, in an obscure place, then his eyes sparkle exceedingly: the child, seeing this, and supposing it to be a piece of crystal, or precious stone, puts forth his hand to take it. What would be very dangerous at another time, shall be safe in the days of the Messiah; for the serpent will not hurt the child."
entries.fb3e5c331a9faa7053031ef6bf3a27e08866adca: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27034" type="x-p"/> A root of Jesse, which shall stand etc. "The root of Jesse, which standeth," etc. - St. John hath taken this expression from Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.5">Rev 5:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rev.22.16">Rev 22:16</reference>, where Christ hath twice applied it to himself. Seven MSS. have עומד omed, standing, the present participle. Radix Isaei dicitur jam stare, et aliquantum stetisse, in signum populorum. - Vitringa. "The root of Jesse is said to stand, and for some time to have stood, for an ensign to the people." Which rightly explains either of the two readings. <reference osisRef="Psa.110.1-Psa.110.7">Psa 110:1-7</reference> (note) is a good comment on this verse.
entries.7b645c2c22d21efbaa6eb235d63e730b29f046c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> And it shall come to pass in that day - This part of the chapter contains a prophecy which certainly remains yet to be accomplished. <div eID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> The Lord "Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, thirty-three MSS. of Kennicott's, and many of De Rossi's, and two editions, read יהוה Yehovah. <div eID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27037" type="x-p"/> The islands of the sea - The Roman and Turkish empires, say Kimchi.
entries.451af78976d618cc7199b5f4408ff94f873ca6c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> The adversaries of Judah "And the enmity of Judah" - צררים tsorerim, Postulat pars posterior versus, ut intelligantur inimicitiae Judae in Ephraimum: et potest (צררים tsorerim) inimicitiam notare, ut (נחומים nichumim) poenitentiam, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8">Hos 11:8</reference>. - Secker.
entries.7f4d9edfb9708487bbb173943b0b4c764d036bf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> The Lord - shall smite it in the seven streams "Smite with a drought" - The Chaldee reads החריב hecherib; and so perhaps the Septuagint, who have ερημωσει, the word by which they commonly render it. Vulg. desolabit; "shall desolate." The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Chaldee read הדריכהו hidrichahu, "shall make it passable," adding the pronoun, which is necessary: but this reading is not confirmed by any MS. <div eID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> Here is a plain allusion to the passage of the Red Sea. And the Lord's shaking his hand over the river with his vehement wind, refers to a particular circumstance of the same miracle: for "he caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land," <reference osisRef="Exo.14.21">Exo 14:21</reference>. The tongue; a very apposite and descriptive expression for a bay such as that of the Red Sea. It is used in the same sense, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.2">Jos 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.5">Jos 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jos.18.19">Jos 18:19</reference>. The Latins gave the same name to a narrow strip of land running into the sea: tenuem producit in aequora linguam. Lucan. 2:613. He shall smite the river to its seven streams. This has been supposed to refer to the Nile, because it falls into the Mediterranean Sea by seven mouths: but R. Kimchi understands it of the Euphrates, which is the opinion of some good judges. See the Targum. See below. <div eID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> Herodotus, lib. i, 189, tells a story of his Cyrus, (a very different character from that of the Cyrus of the Scriptures and Xenophon), which may somewhat illustrate this passage, in which it is said that God would inflict a kind of punishment and judgment on the Euphrates, and render it fordable by dividing it into seven streams. "Cyrus, being impeded in his march to Babylon by the Gyndes, a deep and rapid river which falls into the Tigris, and having lost one of his sacred white horses that attempted to pass it, was so enraged against the river that he threatened to reduce it, and make it so shallow that it should be easily fordable even by women, who should not be up to their knees in passing it. Accordingly he set his whole army to work, and cutting three hundred and sixty trenches, from both sides of the river, turned the waters into them, and drained them off."  <chapter eID="Isa.11"/> <div eID="gen27041" type="x-p"/>

entries.a1b1ff3cce1127f36d7108757509606ca6c828b8: <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference> <div eID="gen12963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12964" type="x-p"/> This is the fate of the imperial power of the world. When the axe is laid to it, it falls without hope. But in Israel spring is returning. <hi type="italic">“And there cometh forth a twig out of the stump of Jesse, and a shoot from its roots bringeth forth fruit.”</hi> The world-power resembles the cedar-forest of Lebanon; the house of David, on the other hand, because of its apostasy, is like the stump of a felled tree (<hi type="italic">geza‛</hi>, <hi type="italic">truncus</hi>, from <hi type="italic">gâza‛</hi>, <hi type="italic">truncare</hi>), like a root without stem, branches, or crown. The world-kingdom, at the height of its power, presents the most striking contrast to Israel and the house of David in the uttermost depth announced in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Isa 6:1-13</reference> <hi type="italic">fin</hi>., mutilated and reduced to the lowliness of its Bethlehemitish origin. But whereas the Lebanon of the imperial power is thrown down, to remain prostrate; the house of David renews its youth. And whilst the former has no sooner reached the summit of its glory, than it is suddenly cast down; the latter, having been reduced to the utmost danger of destruction, is suddenly exalted. What Pliny says of certain trees, “<hi type="italic">inarescunt rursusque adolescunt, senescunt quidem, sed e radicibus repullulant</hi>,” is fulfilled in the tree of Davidic royalty, that has its roots in Jesse (for the figure itself, see F. V. Lasaulx, <hi type="italic">Philosophie der Geschichte</hi>, pp. 117-119).
