(<reference osisRef="Bible:John.3.14">John 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.21.9">Numbers 21:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen42218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42219" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Shall be sought by the Gentiles. </hi>Christ is said to be <hi type="italic">sought</hi>, when men flee to him for the purpose of asking salvation, as to <hi type="italic">seek God</hi> means, in every part of Scripture, to cast all our hopes upon him. Accordingly, the Greek translators have rendered it <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐλπιοῦσι</foreign>, <hi type="italic">they shall hope</hi>, looking rather at the meaning than at the word.<div eID="gen42219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42220" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And his rest shall be glory.</hi> These words are commonly explained as referring to the burial of Christ, and that by a figure of speech in which a part is taken for the whole; for afterwards they apply it also to his death; and indeed the burial of Christ was nothing else than an appendage to his death. They think that the meaning is this, “The death of Christ, which was disgraceful in the eyes of the world, will be <hi type="italic">glorious</hi> and splendid.” But when I take a closer view of the whole, by <hi type="italic">rest</hi> the Prophet means in this passage the Church; as it is also said,<div eID="gen42220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42221" type="x-p"/>This is my everlasting rest; here will I dwell.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.14">Psalm 132:14</reference>.)<div eID="gen42221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42222" type="x-p"/>He bestows an honorable appellation on the assembly of the godly, because he chooses to have a continual habitation among them. Accordingly, the Church having been at that time exposed to reproaches and disgrace, he promises that it will be again raised to a more prosperous condition, and will recover its ancient <hi type="italic">glory</hi>. Here, therefore, we have a remarkable proof that God is pleased to dwell continually in his Church, though this may not always be seen by men.<div eID="gen42222" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42215" osisID="Isa.11.10" type="section"/>
entries.4b504ea895b6d483d519a3e743c7c2ce74c57ced: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.11.11" sID="gen42223" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11. </hi><hi type="italic">And it shall be in that day, the Lord will again set his hand.</hi> The prediction about the future glory of the Church having been incredible, he explains the method of restoring it, namely, that God will display the power of <hi type="italic">his hand</hi>, as if for performing a memorable and uncommon exploit. Now, to confirm the hope of the elect people, he recalls to their minds the remembrance of a past deliverance, that they may not doubt that God is as able to deliver them now as their fathers found him to be in Egypt. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.51">Exodus 12:51</reference>.) Such is the import of the word <foreign xml:lang="he">שנית</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">shenith</hi>,) that is, <hi type="italic">the second time</hi>, or <hi type="italic">again</hi>; as if he had said, “<hi type="italic">Now also</hi> will God be the deliverer of his Church.”<div eID="gen42224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42225" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To possess the remnant of his people.</hi> He confirms what he has said by another argument; for though it appeared as if God had disregarded his people, yet he will not allow himself to be deprived of his inheritance. We may sum it up by saying, that God will take care of the salvation of his Church, so as not to be robbed of his right. He expressly calls them a <hi type="italic">remnant</hi>, because this deliverance belonged only to a small seed. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.9 Bible:Isa.10.22">Isaiah 1:9,10:22</reference>.) In short, he repeats what he formerly said, “Though God disperse and scatter his Church, yet it is impossible that he can ever cast it away altogether; for it is as dear to him as our inheritance is to any of us.”<div eID="gen42225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42226" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Which shall be left from Assyria and from Egypt.</hi> He speaks not only of the <hi type="italic">Assyrians</hi>, who had led the people captive, but also of other nations among whom the Jews were scattered; for though the greater part of the people was carried to Babylon, some fled into <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi>, some into Ethiopia, and some into other countries. They were afraid lest they should endure the same bondage as had been endured by others. Some think that by <hi type="italic">Pathros</hi> is meant <hi type="italic">Parthia</hi>, which is highly probable; others think that it is Arabia the Rocky. Under the name <hi type="italic">Elam</hi> he includes the Medes, Zocdians, Bactrians, and other eastern nations. <hi type="italic">Shinar</hi> belongs to Chaldea. By <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi> they mean Cilicia, and the other countries which lie towards Mount Taurus. By the word <hi type="italic">islands</hi> the Jews mean all countries that lie beyond the sea; for to them Greece, and Italy, and Spain, were islands, because they were separated from them by the sea. <note n="187"> <div sID="gen42227" type="x-p"/> “Not <hi type="italic">islands</hi> merely, but all distant regions are comprised in the meaning of this word <foreign xml:lang="he">איי</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">iye</hi>.)” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi><div eID="gen42227" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen42226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42228" type="x-p"/>We see that the Prophet speaks here not only of the deliverance which took place under Zerubbabel, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.2">Ezra 2:2</reference>,) but that he looks beyond this; for at that time the Israelites were not brought back from Egypt, Ethiopia, and other countries. These words, therefore, cannot be understood to relate to the deliverance from Babylon, but must be viewed as referring to the kingdom of Christ, under whom this deliverance was obtained through the preaching of the gospel. Besides, it is proper to observe that this work belongs to God, and not to men; for he says, <hi type="italic">The Lord shall stretch out his arm</hi>; thus ascribing to his heavenly power this work, which could not have been accomplished by human ability.<div eID="gen42228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42229" type="x-p"/>It ought also to be observed, that from God’s past benefits we ought always to entertain good hopes for the future; so that whenever we call to remembrance the deliverances from Babylon and from <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.2">Ezra 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.51">Exodus 12:51</reference>,) we may be convinced that God is equally able, and will equally assist us at the present day, that he may restore the Church to her ancient glory. What he did once and again, he is able to do a third time, and a fourth, and many times. When the Prophet calls those whom he rescues <hi type="italic">a remnant</hi>, let us learn that we ought not to desire a vast multitude, and let us be satisfied, though we be few, and let us not be terrified by the smallness of our numbers; for, provided that the righteousness of God abound, we have true and abundant ground of confidence.<div eID="gen42229" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42223" osisID="Isa.11.11" type="section"/>
entries.2533ba21c88972bdff95cbb22b2f2f1eb93a53f1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.11.12" sID="gen42230" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">And he will lift up an ensign to the nations</hi>. This verse contains nothing more than the explanation of the former verse. The language is metaphorical, and admits of two meanings; either that, <hi type="italic">by giving an ensign</hi>, he will terrify adversaries, so that they will not dare to prevent his people from returning, or that he will <hi type="italic">give an</hi> <hi type="italic">ensign</hi> to the wretched exiles not to hesitate to make preparations for their return. But even at the present day this doctrine is highly useful among us; for as an <hi type="italic">ensign</hi> is lifted up in the army, that the soldiers may assemble, and that every one may follow and may keep his proper place, so a <hi type="italic">banner</hi> is here held out to us, that we may assemble to it, namely, the gospel, which the Lord has lifted up among the Gentiles, by which Christ is preached to us. <note n="188"> <div sID="gen42232" type="x-p"/> “Set up his standard on an eminence, the signal for the soldiery to assemble round their commander. Caesar terms it <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">vexillum</hi> <hi type="italic">proponere, quod erat insigne, cum ad arma concurri oporteret</hi></foreign>. B. Gall. See Ammian, Hist., 27:10.” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi>.<div eID="gen42232" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen42231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42233" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And will gather together the dispersions of Judah.</hi> Hence we ought to conclude, that we cannot be <hi type="italic">gathered</hi> by the Lord unless we assemble to this <hi type="italic">ensign</hi>, and be joined to him by faith; for there is no other way in which he acknowledges us to be <hi type="italic">his sheep</hi>, than when, after having been <hi type="italic">scattered</hi>, we are <hi type="italic">gathered together</hi>, and meet in the same assembly under this <hi type="italic">ensign</hi>; as he says,<div eID="gen42233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42234" type="x-p"/>My sheep hear my voice and follow me. (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.10.27">John 10:27</reference>.)<div eID="gen42234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42235" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">gather</hi> is repeated. <hi type="italic">He will gather together the outcasts of Israel, and will gather together the dispersions of Judah.</hi> He shows how efficacious God’s calling will be; for as soon as he shall give the slightest indication that such is his pleasure, he will restore the people. <hi type="italic">Dispersion</hi> is a collective noun, for it means the Jews <hi type="italic">scattered</hi> in all directions; and he appears to allude, as he often does elsewhere, to similar passages in the writings of Moses, in which the Lord promises that he will gather the people, though they were scattered to the farthest parts of the world, and to the four winds of heaven. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.30.3 Bible:Deut.30.4">Deuteronomy 30:3, 4</reference>.) Now, this was done under the direction of Christ. Under the same leader we ought at the present day to expect the restoration of a wretched and <hi type="italic">scattered</hi> Church; for there is no hope of <hi type="italic">gathering the remnant</hi> but by the elect looking to this <hi type="italic">ensign</hi>. We ought frequently, therefore, to call to remembrance those promises, that by relying on them we may more and more strengthen our hearts.<div eID="gen42235" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42230" osisID="Isa.11.12" type="section"/>
entries.3d730ccd409095b65976a628147279bb79b994b4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.11.13" sID="gen42236" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the envy of Ephraim shall depart.</hi> Here he promises that the Church will be in such a state of peace, that neither will the Israelites and the Jews contend in civil broils, nor will they suffer any annoyance from their enemies, and that they will not be liable to hatred or <hi type="italic">envy</hi>, as they formerly were. Not that there will be no wicked men, but the Lord will at length cut off and destroy them. But we ought chiefly to observe what he adds about allaying domestic quarrels, that henceforth the children of Abraham may not harass each other, but unite in the same religion, and in the pure worship of God; for it was a disgraceful and shocking spectacle that their mutual strife and hostilities had been so long maintained.<div eID="gen42237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42238" type="x-p"/>With good reason does he point out the source of quarrels, namely, <hi type="italic">envy</hi>, in consequence of which the descendants of Abraham have torn each other, while the tribes of <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ephraim</hi> strive with each other for renown. This horrible torch has always kindled wars in the world, while every man is unwilling to yield. In short, the Lord here promises outward and inward peace, which is a very great and most desirable blessing.<div eID="gen42238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42239" type="x-p"/>It will be objected that this was never accomplished, and that the very opposite of this took place; for as soon as the gospel began, it was followed by various wars, commotions, and dreadful persecutions, and nearly the whole world was disturbed and shaken. And inwardly what peace did the Church enjoy? Among Christians themselves, Satan, by his <hi type="italic">tares</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.25">Matthew 13:25</reference>,) has raised up dreadful disturbances, so that no enemies were more ferocious and destructive than those which were brought up in the bosom of the Church.<div eID="gen42239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42240" type="x-p"/>I reply, the Prophet here includes the whole of Christ’s kingdom, and not merely a single age or century. In this world we taste but the beginning of Christ’s kingdom; and while the Church is harassed by enemies both within and without, still the Lord defends and preserves her, and conquers all her enemies. Besides, this prediction properly belongs to the true and lawful children of Abraham, whom the Lord has purified by the cross and by banishment, and has constrained to lay aside ambition and <hi type="italic">envy</hi>; as those who have been tamed in the school of Christ cease to be desirous of renown. Thus the promise which Isaiah makes in this passage has already been in part fulfilled, and is fulfilled every day. But we must proceed in these exercises, and must fight earnestly within and without, till we obtain that everlasting peace which it will be our happiness to enjoy in the kingdom of God.<div eID="gen42240" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42236" osisID="Isa.11.13" type="section"/>
entries.34559bc61154ab5502ce5daf23b5e9446a7d0f98: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.11.14" sID="gen42241" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14. </hi><hi type="italic">And they shall fly on the shoulders of the Philistines.</hi> He means that there is also another way in which the Lord will assist his people; which is, that he will conquer their enemies, and subdue them under his dominion. Having spoken of the safety of the Church, he now declares that she will be victorious over her enemies. He mentions those nations with which the Jews incessantly carried on wars; for on the one hand the <hi type="italic">Philistines</hi>, and on the other the <hi type="italic">Ammonites</hi> and <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>, to whom they were bound by the tie of relationship and kindred, were continually molesting and attacking them. On one side also were the <hi type="italic">Edomites</hi>, who were not restrained by blood-relationship from being most determined enemies; for they were descended from Esau, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.25 Bible:Gen.25.26 Bible:Gen.36.1 Bible:Gen.36.8 Bible:Gen.36.9">Genesis 25:25, 26, 36:1,8, 9</reference>,) the brother of Jacob; and the remembrance of this ought to have dissuaded them from enmity and hatred. The Lord, therefore, promises that the Church, though she is not absolutely without enemies, will gain advantage over them by suffering, and in the end be victorious.<div eID="gen42242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42243" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Edom and Moab</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">the stretching out of the hands.</hi> <note n="189"> <div sID="gen42244" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">They shall lay their hand upon Edom and Moab</hi>. (Heb. <hi type="italic">Edom</hi> <hi type="italic">and Moab</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">the laying on of their hand</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42244" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">The stretching out of the hands</hi> means the dominion which the Church obtained over her enemies; for by the word <hi type="italic">hand</hi> is usually meant power; and the Hebrews use the phrase, <hi type="italic">to stretch out the hand</hi>, instead of “to place this or that under subjection.” Thus it is said,<div eID="gen42243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42245" type="x-p"/>I will set his hand in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.25">Psalm 89:25</reference>.)<div eID="gen42245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42246" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The stretching out of the hand</hi>, therefore, is full power to rule; and, on the other hand, he adds the <hi type="italic">obedience</hi> which the enemies will yield to her: <hi type="italic">and the children of Ammon </hi>shall be <hi type="italic">their obedience</hi> <note n="190"> <div sID="gen42247" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">And the children of Ammon shall obey them</hi>. (Heb. <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">children of Ammon their obedience</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42247" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen42246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42248" type="x-p"/>The Jews, who dream of an earthly kingdom of Christ, interpret all this in a carnal sense, and apply it to I know not what external power; but they ought rather to judge of it according to the nature of Christ’s kingdom. Partly, no doubt, the accomplishment of this prediction was seen, when the Jews returned from captivity, and God brought them into moderate prosperity, contrary to the wish, and in spite of the opposition, of all the neighboring nations; but believers were led to expect a more splendid victory, which they at length obtained through the preaching of the gospel. Although we must continually fight under the cross, yet we vanquish our enemies, when we are rescued from the tyranny of the devil and of wicked men, and are restored to liberty by Christ, that the flesh may be subdued, and our lusts laid low, and that thus we may live to him, and <hi type="italic">in patience may possess our souls</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.21.19">Luke 21:19</reference>,) calmly and patiently enduring everything that happens. And thus we even <hi type="italic">heap coals on the head</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.20">Romans 12:20</reference>) of enemies, to whose attacks and reproaches we appear to be subject.<div eID="gen42248" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42241" osisID="Isa.11.14" type="section"/>
entries.9c409e098546994c3417ca328dc6398860da65d0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.11.15" sID="gen42249" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the Lord will utterly destroy.</hi> In this verse he means nothing else than that the Lord, by his amazing power, will open for his people a way, which formerly appeared to be shut up. He speaks figuratively. What he calls a <hi type="italic">tongue</hi> is “a bay of the sea;” for when the sea penetrates into the land, and occupies a part of it, there is a resemblance to a person putting out his <hi type="italic">tongue</hi>. He therefore means <hi type="italic">the Egyptian sea</hi> and <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi> itself, as he afterwards more fully explains. But he chiefly mentions <hi type="italic">the sea</hi> and the <hi type="italic">rivers</hi>, because they protect the countries and shut up every entrance.<div eID="gen42250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42251" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And will stretch out the hand over the river in the strength of his wind.</hi> He undoubtedly means the Nile, which waters the whole of Egypt, and divides it into many parts, and might thus interrupt the march of the people when returning to their native country. I have no doubt that <foreign xml:lang="he">רוח</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ruach</hi>) here denotes <hi type="italic">wind</hi>, though he adds <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">Lord’s</hi>; for all the <hi type="italic">winds</hi> are <hi type="italic">the Lord’s</hi>, because he regulates and guides according to his pleasure; and more especially this phrase is employed when it is miraculously agitated by a violent whirlwind. He alludes to the former deliverance of his people, by which he brought them out of <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi>; for when the Lord was pleased to open up a way for them, he dried up the sea by the force and violence of <hi type="italic">the winds</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.14.21">Exodus 14:21</reference>.)<div eID="gen42251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42252" type="x-p"/>True, the Lord did not need the assistance of <hi type="italic">the winds</hi>, for he might have done it by an immediate exertion of his power. But when he makes use of outward means, let us learn, first, that all creatures are ready to yield obedience to him; for though they have a natural course, yet they are in his power, so that he can direct their force and violence in whatever way he pleases. For instance, when a wind arises, its beginning proceeds from a natural cause, and each of the winds has its properties. The south wind is moist, and the north wind is cold, and completely similar are the effects which proceed from them; for the south wind moistens bodies, and the north wind dries them. By extraordinary miracles the Lord shows that he possesses an authority far above these natural causes, so that they are governed, not by nature, (that is, by that succession of events or chain of causes which irreligious men imagine to exist,) but by God alone.<div eID="gen42252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42253" type="x-p"/>Secondly, he shows that he changes the nature and order of events whenever he pleases, that he may be acknowledged to be their only Lord; because such a change exhibits more clearly his authority and dominion. On this account Isaiah called it not simply <hi type="italic">the wind</hi>, but <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">wind of the Lord</hi>, that we may perceive that it is not directed or moved by chance, but by the power <hi type="italic">of the Lord</hi>.<div eID="gen42253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42254" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And shall smite it in the seven streams.</hi> Some render it <hi type="italic">torrents</hi>, and explain it thus: “he will divide the Nile into <hi type="italic">seven</hi> parts.” Though this exposition has been universally adopted, yet I do not approve of it; and I think that it has arisen from forgetfulness, rather than from ignorance, on the part of its authors, who are learned men notwithstanding, and deeply skilled in the perusal of the ancient writers. It is well known from history that the Nile had <hi type="italic">seven</hi> mouths. There are others which are little mentioned, because they had no names, and are therefore called false mouths. Whatever, then, is the number of the mouths or branches, it appears to form that number of <hi type="italic">streams</hi> or rivers; and these might have been so many hinderances to retard their journey. The Prophet expressly mentions them, because the river was highly celebrated.<div eID="gen42254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42255" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And shall make them be shod with shoes.</hi> <note n="191"> <div sID="gen42256" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">And make</hi> men <hi type="italic">go over dry-shod</hi>. (Heb. <hi type="italic">in shoes</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42256" type="x-p"/> </note> The river being deep, he says that he will dry it up, so that it will not be necessary to pull off their <hi type="italic">shoes</hi> in crossing it, though this would have been necessary if only a small portion of water had remained.<div eID="gen42255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42257" type="x-p"/>By these metaphors, therefore, the Prophet means nothing else than that nothing will stand in God’s way, when it shall be his pleasure to rescue his people from captivity. He glances at the history of a former deliverance, that they may learn that it will be the same with that which they formerly enjoyed. On this account he wished to place it, as it were, before their eyes; for the means of this deliverance was not seen. If this promise had been stated in plain terms, it might not have produced so deep an impression on their minds as by holding out this remarkable example.<div eID="gen42257" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.11.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42249" osisID="Isa.11.15" type="section"/>
entries.ac52f2facd483fddc5d8f7307dcfb1ee2c1e8df6:
16. And there shall be a path.
An highway. — Eng. Ver.
This verse contains nothing new, but explains the former verse. The people would perceive the same power of God in the deliverance from Babylon as they had perceived in the deliverance from Egypt. He had opened up a way through seas, (Exodus 14:29; Psalm 77:19,) through untrodden deserts, (Deuteronomy 8:2, 29:5,) and through Jordan; (Joshua 3:16, 17.) In like manner, Isaiah says, that by an unexpected and astonishing method he will again open up a way for his people to go out. Accordingly, what the Lord has once performed let us also expect for the future; and for that purpose let us ponder the ancient histories. This ought also to direct our thoughts to the final deliverance of the Church, by which we shall all be delivered from all troubles and distresses; so that, though what we are told about a resurrection and immortal life may appear to be incredible, and the means of accomplishing them are not seen by us, still the Lord will easily find a way.
CHAPTER 12
Isaiah Chapter 12:1-6
1. And in that day thou shalt say, O Lord, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me.
1. Et dices in die illo: Cantabo tibi Iehova, Tametsi iratus es mihi, aversus est furor tuus, et consolatus es me.
2. Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
2. Ecce Deus salus mea: confidam, et non pavebo. Quoniam fortitudo mea et canticum Deus Iehova; factusque est (vel erit) mihi in salutem.
3. Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation.
3. Haurietis aquas cum gaudio, de fontibus salvatoris (vel, salutis).
4. And in that day shall ye say, Praise the Lord, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted.
4. Et dicetis in die illa: Canite Iehovae; invocate nomen ejus; celebrate in populis opera ejus; commemorate, quia nomen ejus exaltatum est.
5. Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth.
5. Psallite Iehovae, quoniam magnifica gessit; et hoc vulgatum est per totam terram.
6. Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion: for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee.
6. Jubila et canta habitatrix Sion; quia magnus in medio tui Sanctus Israel.

entries.ee864dce19388b31879c02ea2e78280e6a7a9d0b:

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zech. 6. 12. Revel. 5. 5.</ns0:note> there shall come forth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Prophet having dispatched the <ns0:hi>Assyrian,</ns0:hi> and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />forted God's People with the Promise of their Deliverance from that formidable Enemy, now he proceeds further, and declares, That God will do greater things than that for them, that he will give them their long-expected and much<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />desired <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and by him will work Wonders of Mercy for them. For this is the manner of the Prophets, to take the occasion of particular Deliverances, to fix the Peoples Minds upon their great and everlasting Deliverance from all their enemies by the <ns0:hi>Messiah.</ns0:hi> And having said that the <ns0:hi>Assyrian yoke should be destroyed because of the anointing, ch.</ns0:hi> 10. 27. he now more particularly explains who that anointed Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son was.</ns0:note> a rod <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>twig,</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>a branch</ns0:hi> in the next Clause<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Parents are oft compared to Roots or Trees, and their Children to Branches.                         <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the Ten Tribes, frequently called by the name of <ns0:hi>Ephraim,</ns0:hi> as hath been already and frequently ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served, between whom and <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> there were great Emula<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions and Contentions.</ns0:note> shall de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />part <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Of Enemies they shall be made Friends, and of Wolves, Lambs; as was said before on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. they shall be united together in one Church, under the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> keeping the Unity of the Spirit in the Bond of Peace.</ns0:note>, and the adversaries of Judah <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Not the Body of <ns0:hi>Ephraim,</ns0:hi> for they are supposed to be reconciled, and they shall not be cut off, but live in love with <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> as we see by the next Clause; but those few of them which possibly may continue in their Enmity against them, together with all the rest of their Adversa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries.</ns0:note> shall be cut off: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9. 21.</ns0:note> Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Not onely all outward Hostilities shall cease, but also their inward Animosities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And the LORD shall utterly destroy <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Shall not onely divide it, as of old, but will quite dry it up, that it may be an High-way, as it is explained in the next Verse.</ns0:note> the tongue of the Egyptian sea <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The Red Sea, which may well be cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>the Egyptian Sea,</ns0:hi> both because it borders upon <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> and because the <ns0:hi>Egyptians</ns0:hi> were drowned in it<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which is cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>a tongue</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Text, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 15. 2, 5. as having some resemblance with a Tongue: for which reason the name of <ns0:hi>tongue</ns0:hi> hath been given by Geographers to Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />montories of Land which shoot forth into the Sea, as this Sea did shoot out of the Main Ocean into the Land.</ns0:note>, and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He alludes to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his shaking of his Hand with the Rod of God in it over the Sea.</ns0:note> over the river <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, of <ns0:hi>Egypt, Nilus,</ns0:hi> as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears both from the foregoing and from the following Words.</ns0:note>, and shall smite it in the seven streams <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For which <ns0:hi>Nilus</ns0:hi> is famous in all Authors, and by which it emptieth it self into the Sea.</ns0:note>, and make <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> go over <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
